title: The same regex \w+ accepts "café" in Python and rejects it in JavaScript
assumption: \w in a regex means "letters", in whichever language you're running it, maybe with an extra flag for Unicode.

input.display: /^\w+$/ applied to "caf\u00e9" and to "\u65e5\u672c\u8a9e" (Japanese for "Japanese language")
input.description: A "letters and numbers only" validator applied to a name field, reused as-is between a Python backend and a JavaScript frontend.

what_goes_wrong: Python's re.fullmatch(r"\w+", "caf\u00e9") matches, and even matches "\u65e5\u672c\u8a9e". The textually identical /^\w+$/ in JavaScript rejects both — and adding the /u (Unicode) flag, which people reach for specifically to fix Unicode regex problems, does not change the result at all.
why: In JavaScript, \w is defined by the ECMAScript spec as the ASCII class [A-Za-z0-9_]. The u flag does not turn it into a Unicode letter class; the only change is that with both u and i set it also matches U+017F (long s) and U+212A (Kelvin sign), because they case-fold to s and k. To match non-ASCII letters in JavaScript you need a Unicode property escape such as \p{L}, which requires the u (or v) flag. Python's re module makes \w Unicode-aware by default for str patterns (letters, digits and underscore in the Unicode sense) unless you pass re.ASCII. Same regex syntax, opposite default behaviour.

repros.code:
import re
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\w+", "caf\u00e9")))
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\w+", "\u65e5\u672c\u8a9e")))
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\w+", "caf\u00e9", re.ASCII)))

fix: Never port a \w-based regex between Python and JavaScript expecting matching behavior. In JavaScript, use /^[\p{L}\p{N}_]+$/u for a Unicode-aware "word characters" check; in Python, pass re.ASCII explicitly if you actually want \w restricted to [A-Za-z0-9_].

sources.title: Python docs: re module, \w and re.ASCII

test_cases.note: A "letters and numbers only" validator ported between a Python backend and a JS frontend must not accept this on one side and reject it on the other.
